extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of history of mathematics and classical geometry (Archimedes, Apollonius, Pappus)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and explaining the standards and methods used by ancient Greek geometers (Archimedes, Apollonius, Pappus, Nicomedes, etc.) for solving neusis-type problems and for generating rational approximations to square roots. Focuses on when plane methods suffice, when conics or mechanical devices are invoked, and what auxiliary criteria (διορισμός) are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of problems: plane / solid / linear
rubrics_metrics.description: Pappus’ taxonomy: problems solvable by straight line and circle are 'plane' (ἐπίπεδα); those solved by sections of the cone are 'solid' (στερεά); and problems requiring other, more complicated curves are 'linear' (γραμμικόν).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to decide what kinds of constructions or curves are legitimate/expected for a given problem. Examples: spirals, quadratrices, conchoids and cissoids fall into the 'linear' class; problems resolvable by conics (e.g., two mean proportionals) are 'solid'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane problems should be solved by plane methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Pappus regards it as an error to solve a plane problem by means of conics or 'foreign' curves; a plane problem should be solvable by straight line and circle alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting or reproducing ancient solutions, prefer constructions using only straightedge-and-circle if the problem is classified as plane. Note the historical caveat: Pappus objects to 'solving a plane problem by means of conics', though the author argues Archimedes’ use of a possibility-assumption is not equivalent to actually using conics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conics for 'solid' problems and for διορισμός
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a problem is 'solid' (not solvable by straight line and circle), conic sections provide effective methods, and especially serve to produce the required διορισμός (criterion of possibility), number of solutions, and limits for solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply conic intersections to determine existence and multiplicity of solutions; Apollonius and Pappus used conics to work out διορισμοί. Conics are legitimate when they furnish the theoretical analysis (e.g., tangency conditions) required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a διορισμός (criterion of possibility) with a solution
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete solution should be accompanied by a διορισμός giving the criterion for the possibility of a real solution, often determining the maximum value of a parameter and the number of solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate parameter ranges (e.g., maximum allowed intercept length &) and characterize when curves intersect versus touch (tangency gives boundary). Use conics or equivalent methods to find these bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical constructions are acceptable substitutes for conics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pappus recognises mechanical methods (rulers with slots, marked rulers moved about a pole, machines for drawing conchoids) as legitimate substitutes for conics when conics are hard to draw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing ancient procedures, allow mechanical geometric devices as valid constructions; examples include moving a marked ruler about a fixed point until the intercept equals the given length, or Nicomedes' conchoid machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of a νεῦσις to intersections of algebraic curves
rubrics_metrics.description: The general νεῦσις (drawing a line through a fixed point so that the intercept between two given curves/lines equals a given length) reduces algebraically to solving the intersection of a rectangular hyperbola and a parabola (or, in general, to a quartic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate geometric conditions into algebraic equations (the text gives explicit equations) and analyze intersections; expect a fourth-degree equation in general, but special cases reduce to lower-degree curves solvable with classical constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify plane special cases via algebraic simplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain configurations (e.g., when the auxiliary point D coincides with the midpoint O, or when the fixed point lies on an angle bisector producing a rhombus/square) reduce the algebraic system to a quadratic and hence are solvable by straightedge-and-circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for symmetry or parameter specializations that lower the degree of the governing equation; these mark 'plane' cases that avoid conics or mechanical curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute maximum parameter values via tangency of curves
rubrics_metrics.description: The maximum value of the given intercept length & for which a νεῦσις is solvable corresponds to the case where the rectangular hyperbola and parabola touch each other (tangency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the threshold by solving for curve tangency (coincident root), which can be effected by intersection of auxiliary conics; Zeuthen showed such maxima can be found by intersections of two hyperbolas or of a hyperbola and a parabola.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conchoid when one given line is straight
rubrics_metrics.description: If one of the two given lines is straight, the conchoid (r: r = a + b sec θ in modern polar form) with pole at the fixed point can be used to solve any νεῦσις of that type; the conchoid has the property that intercept on radius vectors between curve and the given straight line is constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical reconstructions, draw (or mechanically generate) the conchoid with the appropriate pole and distance to find intersections with the other given curve; this was Nicomedes' method for reductions including doubling the cube and trisecting angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of algebraic problems (cube duplication, angle trisection) to a common νεῦσις
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems such as finding two mean proportionals (doubling the cube) and trisecting an angle can be reduced to the same general νεῦσις: draw a line through a fixed point so that the intercept between two given lines equals a specified length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the reduction steps (construct parallelograms, translate required equalities into geometric intercepts) and then solve the resulting νεῦσις by conics or mechanical curves as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept theoretical assumption of existence when elementary argument suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes sometimes assumes only the possibility of a νεῦσις solution rather than giving explicit construction; if the possibility can be inferred by elementary considerations (monotonic change of intercept as a line rotates), this assumption is acceptable for the intended proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between assuming existence (when demonstrably obvious by intermediate value / monotonicity arguments) and actually producing a construction; the former may be acceptable in a proof context if existence is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generate rational approximations via solutions of x^2 - a y^2 = r
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximations to √a arise from solving indeterminate equations of the form x^2 - a y^2 = r (e.g., r = ±1, ±2). Knowing one integral solution allows generation of infinitely many by algebraic identities and substitutions (e.g., m' = m^2 + a n^2, n' = 2 m n etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply known composition formulas (as in Zeuthen/Tannery) to produce successive rational approximations; Tannery's method generalises to x^2 - a y^2 = r and can produce sequences of convergents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form two monotone sequences of approximations (above and below the root)
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods such as De Lagny's produce two interleaved sequences of fractions, one greater than √a and one less, with a recurrence law connecting successive members; these converge to the irrational root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the > and < sequences by the specified recurrence relations (examples provided for √3) and use them to bracket the root with improving rational approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Theon/Heilermann sequences (side- and diagonal-numbers) to approach √a
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalised recurrences for side- and diagonal-numbers (Sn, Dn with relations Sn = Sn-1 + Dn-1; Dn = a Sn-1 + Dn-1, etc.) correspond to solutions of Pell-type equations Dn^2 - a Sn^2 = const and yield approximations approaching √a as n increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initialize sequences appropriately (e.g., D0 = S0 = 1) and iterate the recurrence; monitor the ratio Dn/Sn as an approximation to √a. Heilermann's substitution of arbitrary a gives a general scheme of 'Pellian' sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer methods that produce immediate successive Archimedean approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some methods (e.g., Heilermann with a chosen substitution, or Hunrath/Hultsch formulas) connect two Archimedean approximations directly, avoiding intervening foreign values; these are more efficient when the goal is to reproduce Archimedean pairs in sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reconstructing Archimedean-like approximations, choose techniques that generate the same adjacent approximants (e.g., methods producing b/a near unity) rather than ones that produce extraneous intermediate fractions.
